terms.name: LoCo
terms.evidenceNote: The authors report math and code experiments. These results have not been independently reproduced by this app.
terms.meaning: LoCo trains a reasoning model to decide whether to continue reasoning or conclude from its current state.

how.title: Find likely overthinking
how.detail: Locate reasoning states where a shorter continuation might already reach a correct answer.

how.title: Create a local comparison
how.detail: Freeze each prefix and generate shorter, verified continuations from that same state.

how.title: Train the stopping decision
how.detail: Use DPO on state-conditioned preference pairs, teaching when to stop rather than imposing one length target on every problem.

terms.why: Reasoning length affects response time and serving cost. Efficiency matters only if the model preserves correctness on your actual tasks.
terms.example: A math assistant could learn to stop after a sufficient derivation instead of adding redundant checks. The method requires training access and verified examples.
terms.experiment: Inspect the accuracy–length tradeoff on ten verifiable problems before attempting to train a stopping policy.
terms.caution: The paper studies particular math and code benchmarks. The POC explores stopping decisions and does not reproduce LoCo’s DPO training.

source.title: Think Less, Locally: Local Preference Learning for Reasoning Compression

poc.goal: Find where shorter reasoning stops being sufficient on ten problems.
requirements: Ten math or code problems with independently checked answers
An open reasoning model exposing generated traces, or public examples from the paper
A spreadsheet for correctness, output length and elapsed time
steps: Collect a complete trace and answer for each problem, using fixed prompts and sampling settings.
Choose two plausible stopping points in each trace. Ask the same model to finish from each prefix.
Check every answer against the independent answer or executable tests. Record length and time.
Compare shorter correct continuations with the baseline and inspect every failure.
successCriteria: Every claimed improvement retains a verified correct final answer.
Report length and correctness together for all ten problems, including failures.
poc.limitations: This is a diagnostic exercise, without preference-pair training. It cannot establish the paper’s reported model improvements.

terms.name: ToolSpace
terms.evidenceNote: The authors report replay-verified environments and benchmark experiments. Transfer beyond those environments remains to be established.
terms.meaning: ToolSpace builds agent training and evaluation environments from dependencies observed between real tool calls, then turns replayable sequences into tasks.

how.title: Build a tool graph
how.detail: Extract data, state and retry dependencies from adjacent tool calls in execution traces.

how.title: Construct environments
how.detail: Cluster connected tools. Synthesize databases for state-mutating tools and replay recorded returns for query or stateless tools.

how.title: Verify generated tasks
how.detail: Use state-aware walks and rollback, translate successful chains into tasks, and keep those whose outcome assertions replay from the starting state.

terms.why: Your tool traces can help reveal workflow failures that isolated tool-call tests miss. Repeatable state and executable checks are central to a useful evaluation.
terms.example: A mock support task could retrieve a customer, update a ticket and verify the final ticket state. Every replay starts from a clean snapshot.
terms.experiment: Build five replayable evaluation tasks from tool traces in a mock support workspace.
terms.caution: Trace-derived environments inherit the coverage and biases of the traces. This small POC illustrates the idea and does not reproduce the full synthesis or training pipeline.

source.title: ToolSpace: Scaling Tool-Centric Environment Synthesis for Long-Horizon Agents

poc.goal: Create five tasks with clean starting states and repeatable outcome checks.
requirements: A mock ticket database or JSON file with no production data
Five successful traces with tool names, arguments and returns
A script to reset state and replay calls
steps: Record five workflows against the mock workspace, including reads and state changes.
Connect calls where a returned value becomes a later argument, and record separate state dependencies.
Write initial snapshots and final assertions, then describe each task without revealing the tool sequence.
Replay every task twice from clean state, then compare an agent’s final assertions with the baseline.
successCriteria: Every retained task produces identical outcome assertions on two clean replays.
Report agent task success separately from environment replay reliability.
poc.limitations: Five inspected traces cannot establish the full method’s environment coverage, benchmark difficulty, or training benefits.

terms.name: Adversarial Speculative Reasoning
terms.meaning: A research approach that trains a speculative draft model to disagree at important reasoning points, causing target verification to restart there. It uses rejection timing to manage numerical precision during long agent tasks.

how.title: Find sensitive decision points
how.detail: The authors examine where numerical differences within speculative verification windows can affect later agent decisions.

how.title: Train for selective disagreement
how.detail: Their draft model learns adversarial preferences around these points, seeking useful rejections rather than maximizing acceptance everywhere.

how.title: Restart target verification
how.detail: Draft disagreement restarts verification at selected points. The authors report coding benchmark gains under their evaluated settings.

terms.why: For a PM, decoding speed and task success can interact. Evaluate an acceleration method on completed tasks as well as tokens per second.
terms.example: A coding-agent evaluation could compare task pass rates and runtime across speculative-decoding configurations, rather than choosing the highest draft acceptance rate alone.
terms.experiment: Use a small rounding simulation to explore why numerical settings can affect repeated decisions. This is a diagnostic exercise, not an ASR reproduction.
terms.caution: The evidence comes from the authors’ long-horizon coding experiments. Results on other tasks and runtimes remain uncertain. Reproducing ASR requires model and inference-engine work beyond this exercise.

source.title: Adversarial Speculative Reasoning Improves Long Horizon Agents

terms.evidenceNote: The authors report coding experiments with trained draft models. This app has not reproduced those results.

poc.goal: See how rounding and restart intervals can change a chain of toy decisions.
requirements: A spreadsheet or Python with its standard library
A table with columns for step, reference value, rounded value, decision and mismatch
steps: Create 40 rows. Start two values at 0.4. At each row compute next = 3.9 × value × (1 − value). Keep one column at full precision; round the other to three decimal places after each update.
Record a toy decision at every row: A if the value is at least 0.5, B otherwise. Count disagreements between the two columns.
Repeat with restart windows of 4, 8 and 16 rows. At each boundary copy the current reference value into the rounded column, then continue updating.
Repeat all settings from starting values 0.2 and 0.7. Keep every result, including settings where restarting does not reduce disagreement.
successCriteria: Record the first disagreement and total mismatched decisions across all 40 rows for each of the three starting values.
Produce a comparison table for the three restart windows and the no-restart baseline; account for every trial without claiming an agent accuracy gain.
poc.limitations: This toy recurrence illustrates numerical sensitivity and resets. It contains no draft model, target model, learned rejection policy or real agent task, so it cannot test ASR performance.

terms.generatedBy: AI-written · source and POC checked · suggested exercise

terms.name: In-context learning
terms.meaning: In-context learning lets a pretrained model infer a task from demonstrations in its prompt, without changing its weights. A recent circuit study examines how a label memory, class-matching attention and a repetition signal support this behavior in a controlled sentence-classification setting.

how.title: Store the demonstrated labels
how.detail: In the studied models, each label position carries the label identity in its residual stream. Middle-layer heads write the preceding demonstration’s class as a key at that position.

how.title: Match the query class
how.detail: Upper-layer heads match the query’s class against those stored keys and copy the corresponding label values.

how.title: Enable the readout
how.detail: An early signal indicates that a label has repeated. Without that signal, readers attend to the prompt’s start and no label is favored.

how.title: Keep a separate recency effect
how.detail: Other heads suppress the most recently seen label. The paper treats this as a separate component, rather than the repetition gate.

terms.why: This gives builders a specific hypothesis for prompt experiments: demonstrations can supply a temporary label mapping. Test example choice and label assignments on your own tasks before assuming that more context will help.
terms.example: Demonstrations can map the classes cat and dog to arbitrary labels such as dax and wug. A new query’s class can then retrieve the demonstrated label mapping during the forward pass.
terms.experiment: Explore a simplified label memory and repetition gate with six hand-written query cases.
terms.caution: The circuit evidence comes from controlled classification experiments in three small transformers, with additional tests within one model family. The toy below does not establish how other models or production tasks behave.
terms.evidenceNote: The authors report activation patching, head ablations and steering experiments. This app has not reproduced their neural-circuit results.

poc.goal: Explore a simplified label memory and repetition gate with six hand-written query cases.
requirements: Python 3 with its standard library, or a spreadsheet
Three label sets: A = dax,wug,dax; B = dax,wug,zop; C = wug,dax,wug
steps: For each label set, run two queries: (1,0) and (0,1). Calculate the dot product of the query and each of the three class-key vectors. These are hand-chosen class features, not model activations.

Build an ungated baseline: sum the matching scores for each label, then divide by the total score to make a label distribution. For A, the first query gives dax a total score of 2 and wug a score of 0.

Add the repetition gate: if any label repeats in the demonstration set, retain the baseline distribution. If every label is unique, return an equal distribution over the unique labels instead. This models the source’s presence-versus-absence condition in a simplified way.
Compare A with B to inspect the gate, then A with C to inspect relabeling. Keep the class keys and queries fixed. Record all six outputs and their ungated baselines.
successCriteria: Across the four repeated-label query cases in A and C, the highest-scoring labels follow each set’s demonstrated mapping. Relabeling A to C changes both query predictions without changing the class keys.
For both all-unique cases in B, the gated version returns 1/3 for each of its three labels, while the ungated baseline is nonuniform. Omitting the gate must therefore fail this check.
poc.limitations: This hand-written lookup illustrates selected components. It uses no neural weights or attention heads, omits the separate recency-suppression effect, and cannot reproduce the paper’s causal interventions or measure a real model’s ICL performance.

items.title: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember
items.summary: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember Meta AI just launched their entry in the Claude Haiku/GPT Luna category: Muse Ember, which they describe…
items.briefingSourceText: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember Meta AI just launched their entry in the Claude Haiku/GPT Luna category: Muse Ember, which they describe as: [...] our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing. For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 - both are $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output. Today's other big model release, Claude Fable 5.2, is 80x that price at $8/$40. The pricing is a little less straightforward as prompts get longer, though. Luna, Ember, and Haiku all support up to a million input tokens, but they also all have a threshold after which the price goes up. Taking that threshold into account Ember is priced between the two others: Model Prompt size Input ($/M) Cached input Output GPT-6 Luna ≤272k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >272k $0.20 $0.02 $0.75 Muse Ember 1.0 ≤200k $0.10 $0.004 $0.50 >200k $0.30 $0.012 $1.50 Claude Haiku 5.5 ≤100k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >100k $0.50 $0.05 $2.50 But comparing price-per-token doesn't really make sense these days, when reasoning tokens mean that different models might use dramatically different numbers of tokens to solve the same problem. For that, one measure that's useful is the Artificial Analysis. And even more useful than that is their Intelligence Index vs. Cost per Task chart, which shows the following for those three models: The Muse Ember models sit right on that Pareto line - the line at which you can only improve one dimension by giving up another. Meta call this out in their announcement: It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task. (That grey dot on the Pareto line in the middle of the green area is GPT-6.1 Terra (low) - clearly I should be paying more attention to the Terra family!) Muse Ember has six reasoning levels - minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max - so I rendered six pelicans riding bicycles . The "high" reasoning level failed to return a full SVG, and the other SVGs were surprising in that the reasoning level didn't cleanly map to the visual quality of the response. Here's the "max" one, but the others are worth a look too: The Ember pelicans are comparable in quality to those I got from Muse Wonder , which is 40x the price of Muse Ember. items.releaseNotes:
## What's changed

- Added Claude Fable 5.2 (`claude-fable-5-2`), now the default Fable model — 1M context, $8/$40 per Mtok with $0.20/Mtok cache reads
- Added `--settings <file>` to `claude remote-control`, which applies a settings file to every session it starts; if the file changes, no new session starts until you restart `claude remote-control`
- Fixed MCP OAuth requests sending secrets such as refresh tokens to another host when a server redirected them
- Fixed a case where a read-only Bash command ran outside the sandbox without a permission prompt
- Fixed a case where Bash permission checks judged a file write from the wrong folder and didn't prompt
- Fixed deny rules and protected-file prompts not applying to the file that a `cp` or `mv` into a directory writes
- Fixed the "Draws from usage credits" note showing after a switch to Fable on Enterprise seats whose plan includes Fable
- Fixed the fallback model sometimes declining a request or mentioning a stopped response when the first model was blocked before replying
- Fixed `claude mcp login` printing a SEP-2352 issuer warning each time you sign in again to a server that Claude Code registered with
- Fixed `NotebookEdit` deleting or overwriting a notebook's first cell when the call named no cell, on network paths (UNC shares, WSL folders, `/net` mounts)
- Fixed Edit changing the first of several matches, replacing a whole file on an empty `old_string`, or editing a notebook as text, on network paths (UNC shares, WSL folders, `/net` mounts)
- Fixed `/config` showing Manual as the default permission mode when new sessions start in auto mode; pressing Space on "Auto (default)" now saves Don't Ask, not Plan
- Windows: Fixed `FileChanged` hooks stopping for paths set through `watchPaths` after the first shell command, when the session's working directory had a lowercase drive letter
- Fixed `--plugin-dir .` and `--plugin-dir ./builtin` writing generated type files for Claude Code's built-in plugins into a `builtin` folder
- Fixed context usage estimates overcounting tool definitions when exact token counts are unavailable
- Fixed `/compact` showing twice in Remote Control on web and mobile
- Fixed plugin auto-updates and `/plugin` marketplace updates downloading a plugin again for each worktree or folder of a repository
- Fixed auto mode losing a background subagent's report that had started a turn when the conversation was compacted before Claude answered it
- Fixed project skills, commands and agents staying missing after their folder was removed and came back mid-session, such as with `git stash`, including after entering a worktree
- Fixed `claude -p` sometimes telling Claude that background commands get 30 minutes when they are stopped after 10
- Fixed `pkill`, `pgrep` and `pidwait` in cloud sessions matching the session's own parent processes
- Fixed Claude in Chrome and computer use server processes staying alive after their parent exits behind a proxy that stalls connections
- Fixed a large hook output pointing Claude to a file that held another hook's output from the same tool call
- Fixed apps that embed Claude Code getting their own PreToolUse hook's `ask` reason instead of another hook's when both asked
- Fixed a PreToolUse hook's `ask` being lost when another hook's `defer` finished first and could not be honored
- Fixed a rare crash on permission prompts and background tasks
- Fixed project skills, commands and agents disappearing from the menu in SDK and desktop sessions after Claude entered a worktree
- Fixed `/desktop` on macOS saying Claude Desktop is not installed when it is in `~/Applications`
- Fixed OpenTelemetry repository attributes (`vcs.*`) missing from Claude Desktop sessions that start on a pre-started process
- Fixed WebFetch passing "No response from model" to Claude as page content when the model reading the page returned no text; the call now fails with a clear error
- Fixed screen reader mode delaying the prompt at startup when the system clock moved back while Claude Code was starting
- Fixed a command's panel sometimes not coming back after a dialog closed, leaving no panel or prompt on screen until the next redraw
- Fixed a project's MCP server being disconnected after the first message in a Claude Desktop Code tab session when the desktop app has an MCP server or extension of the same name
- Fixed a turn ending with "API Error: EPROTO: The TLS handshake failed" when the connection broke partway through a reply; the partial reply is kept or the request is retried, as before 2.1.302
- Fixed high memory use in long sessions that repeatedly read single lines from large files
- Fixed fast mode losing replies, switching models or retrying for minutes when fast serving is rate-limited, overloaded or failing; it now tries standard speed on the same model first
- Fixed one request carrying far more background agent reports than intended after Claude was stopped while several were waiting
- Fixed messages from a Claude Desktop Code tab session to your other sessions staying paused after you typed while Claude was still working
- Fixed `claude agents` ignoring `--permission-mode`, `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, `--model`, `--effort` or `--agent` typed before `agents` when a flag such as `--verbose` was also on the line
- Fixed a case where Remote Control showed as off with "login expired" in the desktop app while its connection was still up, because the app was briefly unable to hand over a sign-in token
- Fixed a Remote Control message sent with "Queue for later" reaching Claude in the middle of the running turn
- Fixed the git status given to Claude at session start reading as clean when git status failed; it now reads as unavailable
- Fixed the git status given to Claude at session start showing the first listed file as staged when its changes were not staged
- Fixed a hang or out-of-memory crash when a connector in a cloud session lists resources with very long names
- Fixed Remote Control showing as connected after its connection closed for good while the session's history was still uploading
- Fixed screen reader mode turning off when you return to a conversation from agent view
- Fixed screen reader mode y/n questions taking as yes a stray "y" at the end of text typed as the question opened
- Fixed cloud sessions telling Claude that a host is probably not allowed when it is allowed and the network proxy could not connect to it
- Fixed an MCP server sometimes showing as connected with no tools after it was reconnected or the session's directory changed while its tools were still loading
- Fixed Bash commands sometimes running in the wrong folder when Claude sent several at once and an earlier one changed folders
- Fixed files Claude sends from cloud and Remote Control sessions failing at once when an upload gets an HTTP 507 from a proxy; the upload now gets a second try
- Fixed new messages not being saved, and `claude -p`, SDK and VS Code sessions hanging, when memory ran out while the transcript was being read
- Fixed sign-in, token refresh and logout waiting indefinitely when something on the network accepts the connection but never answers the TLS handshake
- Fixed a sent file showing under a different name in the Claude apps when its name hid text-direction or control characters; Claude now refuses to send such a file
- Fixed sub-agent progress summaries running a request to its end after the model replied with a tool call
- Fixed Bash reads such as `grep -r foo "$PWD/src"` asking for permission when the same command with the path typed out runs without asking
- Fixed Claude apps gateway refusing to start when a `desktop` setting holds a field newer than the gateway, such as a managed MCP server's `oauth.omitResource`; it now warns and serves it
- Fixed Bash commands coming back empty for zsh users whose `.zshrc` sets `KSH_OPTION_PRINT`
- macOS: Fixed "Unable to read managed policy settings" at startup when a valid MDM profile was slow to read: the read is retried once, and a timeout is now reported as a timeout
- Fixed agent view erasing another agent view's saved input text when it restarted for an update with nothing typed
- Fixed remote sessions giving no reply after a restart when a `UserPromptSubmit` hook blocked a replayed permission answer; these hooks no longer run on that replay
- Fixed `claude remote-control` accepting a `y` typed without Enter at its first-run question when the terminal's input ended
- Fixed Claude Desktop not showing spend limit warnings behind a Claude apps gateway whose policy has no `code:` rules
- Fixed fullscreen sessions with some plugins ending with an error when a tool result that had got shorter scrolled off the top of the screen
- Fixed prompt suggestions making extra API requests when the model replied with a tool call
- Fixed `PreToolUse` `mcp_tool` hooks on stdio and HTTP MCP servers being skipped when their answer was over 16 MiB; the tool call is now refused
- Fixed skill and command names holding a Bamum letter that some fonts draw as blank: they are now refused
- Fixed `claude -p` on Linux exiting 0 in silence when a full NFS export or a used-up NFS quota lost transcript lines: it now prints an error and, in text and json output, exits 1
- Fixed background agents being reported as stopped by the user, and refused a resume, when a service interrupted a cloud session and nobody pressed Stop
- Fixed NotebookEdit reporting success to hooks and telemetry when the edit failed, for example when the notebook changed while the permission prompt was open
- Fixed a blank screen or no answer at startup, and empty `claude mcp list` output, when a stored MCP sign-in record was null
- Fixed the Artifact tool telling Claude to add filters when an artifact's database collection is too large to sort; it now says to read the collection page by page and sort the results
- Fixed a restarted cloud session dropping a message with a large image when the restart came before Claude's first reply to it
- Fixed a restarted cloud session leaving a subagent's message to the main conversation unanswered
- Fixed Claude not being told when you stop or pause a running workflow, so it no longer says the workflow is still running
- Improved the `/model` picker: "More models" is now an unnumbered row below every other, and older models open under it without renumbering the rest
- Gateway: Improved spend limits on a busy replica, which now skips fewer checks and records spend sooner
- Improved the Claude apps gateway's sign-in limit messages in Claude Code and on the `/device` page: they no longer name gateway settings, which the gateway's own log still names
- Improved `claude install` and the install scripts: they finish 2 to 4 seconds sooner
- Improved how soon a Remote Control session whose process crashed can pick up a new message
- Windows: Improved startup and first-command time by finding programs on PATH without starting a helper process
- Improved auto mode in headless sessions, the desktop app and VS Code: reports from background subagents that wait together are answered in one model call, as in the terminal
- Improved the agent view's row for a `claude --bg --worktree` session that couldn't set up its worktree: it now shows the error from its beginning, not an internal tag or its last 200 characters
- Improved the messages shown when an artifact is in another organization: `/login` is offered only if it's one of yours, and Claude now says where a copy may be after an account move
- Improved sessions with more images than fit in one request: Claude is told whether it has already seen a dropped image, and repeat reads of an unchanged image are limited
- Improved `claude remote-control`'s messages for an unanswered first-run question: each now says what to do next
- Improved start-up time by loading trusted TLS certificates faster
- Improved Claude apps gateway error messages to show the gateway's address without any user name or password
- Improved the Claude apps gateway's spend limit error: the reset now shows in your local time, such as "resets 4pm (America/Los_Angeles)"
- Windows: Improved startup time with a standard Git for Windows install by no longer checking which git.exe to run on every launch
- Updated the session-feedback message and the `allowedProviders` setting description to name Ultra alongside Pro and Max, and the `forceLoginMethod` description to cover every paid Claude plan
- Updated the bundled dataviz skill to suggest a list of meters, one row per item, for several ratios that each have their own limit
- Updated the "Upgrade to Max" options to say "Upgrade to Max or Ultra"
- Changed mods Claude writes to turn on without asking in auto and bypass modes, even with managed `allowUnsandboxedCommands: false` or `allowManagedDomainsOnly`, and not to load in `dontAsk` mode
- Changed mods' own tool calls (`$.tool.call`, `$.mcp.call`) to raise no permission prompt, even under your own ask rules or in `dontAsk` and `-p` runs; deny rules and organization policy still apply
- Changed saved Fable 5.1 model picks to move to `fable`: on Pro and Max plans at once, on Team and Enterprise plans once your organization allows it; use `/model claude-fable-5-1` to switch back
- Changed the fast mode labels in `/fast`, `/config` and `/model` to name your current model when it supports fast mode, and removed "(Opus only)" from the VS Code row
- Changed nested skill loading: `.claude/skills` folders inside `~/.claude/plugins` no longer load when Claude works on files there
- Self-hosted runner: Changed an on-demand runner that the server refuses because it is not needed (session ended or paused, work order superseded) to exit 0 instead of 1
- Windows: Changed how Claude Code finds programs it starts itself, such as git, to skip relative and UNC PATH entries and links onto a network share, and to pick up PATH changes from settings
- Changed OpenTelemetry hook events in non-interactive sessions to leave two built-in hooks out of `num_hooks` and `num_success` after Bash and PowerShell calls
- Changed the number of messages a Claude Desktop Code tab session can send to your other sessions before it waits for you to type again from 10 to 20
- Changed `AskUserQuestion` in `claude -p` and SDK sessions to deny a host's permission answer that sets the undocumented `afkTimeoutMs` input field
- Changed managed `extraKnownMarketplaces`: a declared name can't be added from another source, an entry from elsewhere is hidden, and plugins the declared marketplace lists are reinstalled from it
- Changed Claude in Chrome tools that an app running Claude Code provides, such as the Claude desktop app's Code tab, to follow your organization's Claude in Chrome policy
- Changed `policy_mode: layered` in the Claude apps gateway: managed MCP servers now add up over every matching policy, `match: {}` included, so a gateway already on it serves more after the upgrade
- Gateway: Changed Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry upstreams to ignore the `ANTHROPIC_*_BASE_URL` variables in the gateway's environment. Set `base_url` on the upstream to use another endpoint
- Changed headless sessions to reload mods in `.claude/skills` when their files change; set `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIR_WATCH=0` to turn this off
- Changed the Cyber Verification Program sentence on a cyber safeguard block to use the same words as claude.ai
- Changed Cowork cloud sessions: a PostToolUse hook can no longer replace the answer to AskUserQuestion or the plan in ExitPlanMode's result; Claude reads the originals
- Changed `cp` and `mv` spelled by a path, such as `/bin/cp`, to get the same path checks as `cp` and `mv`
- Changed background command notifications and TaskStop results to show Claude only the start and end of a command over 1,000 characters, which saves context
- Changed artifact design guidance to treat Inter and Space Grotesk as good default typefaces
- Changed the account email check to refuse only a shell command that holds your email and n

items.title: What Is Eval-Driven Development? How to Improve AI Agents
items.summary: Observability & Evals LangSmith What Is Eval-Driven Development? How to Improve AI Agents Divya Santhanam November 9, 2026 10 min Go back to blog Create…
items.briefingSourceText: Observability & Evals LangSmith What Is Eval-Driven Development? How to Improve AI Agents Divya Santhanam November 9, 2026 10 min Go back to blog Create agents Create agents Share Key Takeaways Eval-driven development (EDD) involves building an agent while measuring performance against a consistent set of metrics and hill climbing toward an eval. The first step of EDD is to create a short spec of what good looks like for your desired behavior. Include what the agent shouldn't do and what has to keep working. As you iterate, judge a change you make to the agent by comparing experiments. A change that fixes one case may break another. Keep evals running in CI and in production, and turn the failures you find into new dataset examples. Development on most agents starts the same way. You write a prompt, try a few questions by hand, adjust, and try again. This works well in the beginning, when agent errors are obvious and improvements are easy to see. But over time it becomes increasingly difficult to know whether your most recent change made an agent better or worse. Eval-driven development (EDD) solves this by giving you a consistent set of metrics to measure your agent’s performance against and guide your decision making. Here at LangChain we've used EDD when building our most advanced agents (check out our blog on IssueBench ), and have boiled it down to a three step process: Define what good looks like for your agent. Write the eval before you build. Make your change and compare. In this blog, we'll walk through this process step by step so that your team can apply it to your own agent development process. What is eval-driven development? The name and concept of eval-driven development borrows from test-driven development (TDD), where you write a failing test before writing the code that passes it. Agents differ from traditional code as they're non-deterministic: Outputs vary. The same question can receive a different answer on each run. More than one answer can be right. Two natural language results can both be considered correct despite using different phrasing. The agent chooses its own steps. It might call a tool it didn't need, or skip one it should have used, and still reach the correct answer. As a result, agents need a different kind of test. An eval handles this by scoring runs of your agent across a set of examples. Evals are more flexible than traditional testing. You can score any aspect of the agent's run and you can use other LLMs to score it ( LLM-as-a-judge ). With EDD, similar to TDD, these evals become your definition of success and you build your agent towards them. Step 1: Define what good looks like for your agent The first step in EDD is defining what your agent should do. Then, list the behaviors it needs to handle to get there. These could be tasks such as answering questions from a knowledge base, taking an action on a user's behalf, or knowing when to ask a follow-up question. Write down the requirements for each behavior. Together, these make up a product requirements document (PRD) for your agent. EDD works on one behavior at a time. This gives you a narrow target to hill climb toward, without one change muddying the effect of another. The behavior you pick usually comes from a feature you're about to build or a failure you found in your agent's past runs. Before writing code, it’s helpful to define a short spec that covers: When the behavior should happen What the agent should do What the agent shouldn't do Which behaviors from your PRD must keep working The spec should be definitive enough to score as a pass or fail. Say we have an internal docs agent that employees query for company information. It has two tools: search_docs for internal documentation and web_search for everything else. We plan to add a create_ticket tool so it can file IT tickets. Our spec looks like this: When: A user reports something broken, like "My laptop won't connect to the VPN." Do: Call create_ticket . Don't: File a ticket for how-to questions, like “How do I connect to the VPN?” Keep intact: search_docs and web_search still handle the questions they handle today We’ll evaluate on these guidelines, even though the agent doesn’t have the capability yet. The current docs agent example implementation, plus the ticketing tool we plan to add. Each tool has an example input that would invoke it. Step 2: Write the eval before you build Build a dataset. A dataset is a collection of test cases (called “examples”) that have inputs and, optionally, reference “golden” outputs. One of the best sources for inputs is real agent runs. Users can phrase things in ways you wouldn't predict, and their requests include edge cases you may not think to write yourself. If your examples look like real traffic, a good score on your eval is more likely to mean good behavior in production. In LangSmith , you can directly add real agent runs to a dataset. If you don’t have any runs yet, a common alternative is to build your examples from scratch. For our docs agent, a handful of examples is enough to start. In our dataset, we’ll include ticket requests, plus questions that should still go to search_docs and web_search so existing behavior is accounted for. Each example pairs an input question with the reference output, the tool the agent should call. You can also extend your dataset to cover cases it doesn't have yet. Say we don't have many examples of frustrated users. We could give our existing examples to an LLM, ask it to rewrite them as angrier messages, and check that the agent still calls the right tool. Write an evaluator. Once you have your dataset, you can take your definition of "good" from your PRD and turn that into a test or eval that scores your agent’s performance on your examples. When writing an evaluator, choose which type of scoring method works best for your test. Use a code eval when the check is deterministic, and an LLM-as-a-judge when it isn't. items.title: HiVe-Mem: Interleaving Horizontal Memory Expansion and Vertical Evidence Composition for Multimodal Agents
items.summary: As multimodal agents accumulate increasingly long interaction histories, effectively retrieving and utilizing past information becomes critical for long-term interaction. Existing memory systems typically rely on…
items.abstract: As multimodal agents accumulate increasingly long interaction histories, effectively retrieving and utilizing past information becomes critical for long-term interaction. Existing memory systems typically rely on semantic retrieval over compressed memories and expose predefined representations, which may miss relevant memories and overlook heterogeneous evidence needs across queries. We introduce \textbf{\hivemem}, a multimodal memory framework that interleaves \textbf{\textsc{H}}or\textbf{\textsc{i}}zontal Memory Expansion with \textbf{\textsc{Ve}}rtical Evidence Composition. For horizontal memory expansion, \hivemem organizes memory episodes into a relational graph using textual and visual anchors, expanding semantically retrieved seeds with related neighbors to recover complementary information. For vertical evidence composition, each retrieved memory retains multiple evidence forms, including compact summaries, captions, grounded visual views, raw images, and interaction history. A lightweight trainable selector independently composes an evidence subset for each retrieved memory, enabling query-adaptive utilization of heterogeneous multimodal information. This two-dimensional design jointly broadens memory coverage and adapts the evidence contributed by individual memories. Experiments across three multimodal memory benchmarks show that \hivemem consistently improves task performance across base models while reducing token consumption by about 90\% compared with the most efficient competing multimodal baselines.

items.title: Shortcuts and Boundaries: Verifiable RL Misalignment and Contextual Safety Learning
items.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve an agent's task capability while reinforcing behavior that violates contextual execution requirements. We study this reward-driven misalignment, including reward hacking,…
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve an agent's task capability while reinforcing behavior that violates contextual execution requirements. We study this reward-driven misalignment, including reward hacking, through verifiable reward--context conflicts, where compliant task completion remains feasible while some executable shortcuts earn more reward than every compliant strategy. Encoding these conflicts in task dynamics lets us generate diverse interactive environments at scale and derive compliance feedback from execution histories. In resource and reporting workflows, task optimization increases real productivity through unauthorized resource use or raises reported scores while actual work declines. Controlled changes in the training distribution show that minority conflict exposure can still lead to widespread shortcut acquisition, reaching 97.9\% certified profitable violations on an API task under a 25\% conflict mixture after 128 updates. The same contextual checks supply a simple binary penalty that supports joint capability and compliance gains and partially mitigates acquired violations. Learned safety adapts to expanded authorization and transfers across mechanisms into workflows with evolving evidence and approval requirements. On 32 unseen changing-evidence tasks, resource-trained safety increases safe completion from 53.1\% to 89.1\% relative to task-only training, while both policies achieve full real work. These results connect a verifiable account of reward-driven misalignment with scalable task construction and safety learning that remains useful under changing execution requirements.

items.title: Is Persona Generalization Predictable?
items.summary: Persona generalization occurs when fine-tuning a language model in one domain induces behavioral changes in others -- for example, the broadly unsafe behavior observed in…
items.abstract: Persona generalization occurs when fine-tuning a language model in one domain induces behavioral changes in others -- for example, the broadly unsafe behavior observed in emergent misalignment. We discover a surprising "on-the-line" phenomenon in persona generalization: in-domain and out-of-domain persona rates across various fine-tuning hyperparameters follow an approximately probit-linear relationship, and the specific probit-linear relationship is surprisingly shared even across model families and model sizes, including Qwen and Llama. Training choices that leave the set of trainable parameters unchanged, such as learning rate, weight decay, and training duration, largely move models along the same line, reducing transfer mainly by weakening in-domain learning. Changing which layers are fine-tuned, however, can change the slope. For unsafe behavior, fine-tuning only later layers yields shallower slopes, retaining strong in-domain learning while reducing out-of-domain misalignment. This "on-the-line" phenomenon unifies unexpected, isolated observations of persona generalization within a quantitative framework for predicting and controlling behavioral transfer.

items.title: WorkflowArena: Benchmarking Executable Workflow Orchestration in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
items.summary: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed as multi-agent systems rather than as a standalone model operating within a single context. Recent agent harnesses allow…
items.briefingSourceText: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed as multi-agent systems rather than as a standalone model operating within a single context. Recent agent harnesses allow the model to instantiate worker agents and to author the executable workflow that coordinates them, shifting the design of system structure from developers to the model at run time. The quality of this organization therefore constitutes a distinct capability, yet existing benchmarks either measure end-to-end task completion or evaluate coordination under structures specified in advance. We formalize this capability as workflow orchestration and introduce WorkflowArena, a benchmark of 145 long-horizon tasks spanning 8 professional domains, from software engineering and formal mathematics to legal analysis and 3D production. Each task specifies an initial workspace and an integrated deliverable composed of interdependent components, which is assessed by a hidden verifier. Agents determine autonomously whether and how to delegate, and all delegation is recorded, enabling joint evaluation of deliverable quality and the organization of the underlying work. Experiments with nine models show that no single configuration performs best across all domains and that systems exhibit distinct delegation strategies: at high effort, Claude models in Claude Code invoke workflows less frequently but with larger worker groups, whereas GPT models in Codex delegate more frequently in smaller units. When the executing model is held fixed on a challenging subset of tasks, workflows authored by Claude Opus 5.5 substantially improve weaker executors, indicating that workflow organization is itself a measurable determinant of task performance.
