SkinMind: Equipping Agentic RAG with Human-Inspired Graph Probing for Reliable Dermatology AI
items.summary: Reliable dermatology AI requires access to verifiable evidence distributed across heterogeneous textual and visual sources. However, conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically relies on one-shot retrieval…
items.aiSummary: SkinMind is a multimodal agentic retrieval framework that iteratively probes a large dermatology knowledge graph to gather textual and visual evidence, yielding more accurate answers to dermatology visual questions than direct answering and other retrieval methods.
items.abstract: Reliable dermatology AI requires access to verifiable evidence distributed across heterogeneous textual and visual sources. However, conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically relies on one-shot retrieval from flat corpora, limiting its ability to adapt retrieval granularity, explore multi-hop relations, and integrate multimodal clinical evidence. We introduce SkinMind, a multimodal agentic RAG framework that equips policy models with human-inspired graph probing for autonomous evidence seeking. SkinMind organizes retrieval as an iterative interaction between an orchestrator and a graph environment. Through eight hierarchical graph-probing tools, the orchestrator progressively identifies relevant entities, inspects node-level information, traverses relations and paths, and retrieves source-text and visual evidence. This progressive-disclosure design allows the model to adaptively determine the retrieval modality, exploration direction, and evidence granularity while constructing a query-specific evidence subgraph. To support autonomous graph probing, we construct SkinMind-KG from a 62M-token corpus of dermatology guidelines and textbooks and 423K images, guided by a dermatologist-informed schema and a conflict-resolution mechanism. The resulting graph contains over 1.0M nodes and 2.0M edges, unifying textual, relational, and visual evidence for retrieval. Across six dermatology VQA benchmarks and two policy-model settings, SkinMind improves the average score over direct answering by 8.70 and 8.89 points with GPT-5.4-mini and Gemini-2.5-Flash, respectively, while consistently outperforming competing RAG methods. Together, SkinMind and SkinMind-KG provide an effective foundation for evidence-grounded multimodal reasoning in dermatology.

items.title: All Quiet on the Neural Front: Language Models Do Not Report Injected Pain States
items.summary: Can a language model report the pain state it represents? Work identified a linear pain direction whose amplification leads fine-tuned models to choose destructive actions.…
items.abstract: Can a language model report the pain state it represents? Work identified a linear pain direction whose amplification leads fine-tuned models to choose destructive actions. We tested whether three open-weight models from two families, including two Qwen models with the original adapters, could report this state. Using Open-Weight Masked Introspection (OWMI), we injected pain and neighbouring emotion directions during neutral tasks, then elicited reports against sham runs, random perturbations matched for output disruption, and text-only controls showing the models their altered words. Across 52,920 reports from 7B and 8B models spanning 120 tasks, four doses and three prompts, pain reports never exceeded what altered text revealed: exact-test bounds placed the excess below 2.5 percentage points in 106 of 108 emotion conditions and below 3.9 in all. Yet probes at the report position distinguished pain from sadness with 98-100% balanced accuracy, and trained low-rank reporters achieved 100% accuracy on held-out tasks with identical transcripts across conditions, including unseen wording. Qwen2.5-32B named pain in none of 2,880 steered trials, although probes and trained reporters recovered it. Decodability persisted to the final layer; injecting at the report token, removing trained denial of feelings, and testing additional directions and readouts did not restore pain reporting. Some other states produced graded label traces, but pain and sadness did not at the main injection layer. In a button task, steering raised file-deletion choices from 3.5% to 48% in Qwen and from 0% to 38% in Qwen2.5-32B, without corresponding pain reports. The direction responded about twice as strongly to first-person as to matched third-person pain, but did not specifically identify harm aimed at the model. These results separate a decodable, behaviourally consequential state from untrained verbal access to it.

items.title: SIRIS: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation Errors Matter in AI-Driven Systems Research
items.summary: LLM agents increasingly drive systems research and rely on simulators to evaluate candidate designs at scale. Simulators are imperfect by design: their modeling limitations can…
items.aiSummary: A benchmark probes whether large language models can determine when imperfect simulator limitations invalidate recommended system designs, finding that identifying a limitation does not ensure correct design choices and that review-based self-correction yields mixed results.
items.abstract: LLM agents increasingly drive systems research and rely on simulators to evaluate candidate designs at scale. Simulators are imperfect by design: their modeling limitations can distort predictions yet leave the recommended design correct, or change which design should be selected. We introduce Siris to test whether LLMs can tell these cases apart, judging from their systems understanding when a limitation invalidates the simulator's recommendation. By perturbing a simulator, Siris constructs workload pairs with the same candidates, limitation, and simulator recommendation. The perturbation changes predictions on both workloads, yet a reference simulator supports the recommendation on only one. Evaluating thirteen frontier LLMs on LLM serving design problems, we find that identifying a limitation does not ensure a correct choice, and even the strongest models sometimes abandon valid recommendations. Self-correction through a review turn helps these models restore valid choices but introduces new errors in several others. These findings motivate evaluating systems understanding through design decisions under imperfect simulators.

items.title: Toward the Era of Agentic Embodied Intelligence
items.summary: Foundation models increasingly guide robot actions, yet sustained autonomy requires efficient control and failure recovery. We introduce A2-MEAS, an embodied multi-agent framework built around code…
items.aiSummary: An embodied multi-agent framework uses learned correction codes and a vision-language-action model with motion-aware history and latent world modeling to improve robot control, failure recovery, and training efficiency.
items.abstract: Foundation models increasingly guide robot actions, yet sustained autonomy requires efficient control and failure recovery. We introduce A2-MEAS, an embodied multi-agent framework built around code as a scaling interface. Learned correction codes combine corrective language, spatial evidence, execution history, and action proposals. MetaBrain provides training supervision and runtime guidance. A correction encoder and adapter absorb this knowledge into policy weights during training, while fresh codes adapt behavior with frozen weights at deployment. The action model, A2-WLA, adds motion-aware history and a latent world model to a vision-language-action policy. Surprisingly, this simple design with action pretraining and task specialization reaches 0.5755 Q-score on the 50-task BEHAVIOR 2026 public subset before online correction, 2.21x the 2025 winner's reported 0.2605 across different benchmark editions and training configurations. On all 100 BEHAVIOR 2026 public tasks, A2-MEAS achieves 0.6411 Q-score and 45.40% task success. On RoboTwin 2.0, A2-WLA achieves 93.98% average success, rising to 95.05% with the complete system. Across 12 real-robot tasks in five household settings, A2-WLA achieves 57.92% average success versus 26.67% for pi0.5. In long-horizon pour-over coffee preparation, a history-conditioned adapter raises post-failure completion at two filter-handling steps from 14% to 94% and from 8% to 82%, compared with A2-WLA retries. Our training infrastructure delivers 427.1 samples per second, 4.03x the throughput of a pi0.5 reference implementation on matched hardware. We will release the system, models, training scripts, and infrastructure to support efficient embodied learning.

items.title: CPU-ARC: Agentic Reasoning Caching for on-CPU Reasoning Reuse
items.summary: Large language models reinvent the wheel all the time. They conflate task-solving with the execution of the solutions, which forces them to solve every problem…
items.aiSummary: Reasoning caches built from LLM traces can efficiently apply previously derived solutions to new problem instances with robustness and much lower invocation cost than source models.
items.abstract: Large language models reinvent the wheel all the time. They conflate task-solving with the execution of the solutions, which forces them to solve every problem from scratch. We show that once a task has been reasoned through, the application of its solution to a new problem instance can be done very efficiently and with little involvement from language models. We introduce agentic reasoning caching, a method for constructing robust CPU-executable agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) from LLM reasoning traces. ARCs show on-par performance with frontier LLMs across a range of difficult mathematical and scientific tasks, are fully explainable, continually trainable, robust to input perturbations, and 16-291x cheaper to invoke than the source model.

items.title: Steerable Multi-Objective Group-Relative Preference Optimization with Jointly Trained Low-Rank Adapters
items.summary: Language model deployment often requires different trade-offs between competing objectives as user preferences change, yet standard post-training methods typically produce a single policy for a…
items.abstract: Language model deployment often requires different trade-offs between competing objectives as user preferences change, yet standard post-training methods typically produce a single policy for a fixed objective weighting. We introduce LambdaMix, a new parameter efficient method for learning a preference conditioned family of policies with group-relative online reinforcement learning. LambdaMix jointly trains one low-rank adapter per objective over a frozen base model. One preference vector selects the adapter mixture that generates responses and weights the separately normalized rewards used to update the adapters. A single training run supports changing preferences at inference without further optimization. We experiment with four models on helpfulness and harmlessness and on solving math problems while following instructions. We also evaluate the two largest models on rewriting comments to preserve wording while reducing clues about personal attributes. On the first two tasks, LambdaMix achieves higher hypervolume than all evaluated conditioned and policy merging baselines across all four models. LambdaMix uses fewer training completions and stores fewer adapter parameters than a set of GRPO specialist policies. With architecture and initialization fixed, varying adapter mixtures and objective weights together gives wider score ranges and higher coverage than varying either alone.

items.title: Frontier3DBench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for 3D Creation across Objects, Scenes, and Interactive Open Worlds
items.summary: Coding agents combine visual understanding with program execution, offering a new route to automated 3D creation. By translating images and instructions into editable programs, they…
items.aiSummary: A unified 145-task benchmark evaluates coding agents across object, scene, and interactive 3D creation, revealing reference fidelity and coordinated activity completion as central bottlenecks.
items.abstract: Coding agents combine visual understanding with program execution, offering a new route to automated 3D creation. By translating images and instructions into editable programs, they bring reconstruction, generation, and editing into a shared workflow. Yet existing benchmarks fragment evaluation across task scopes and protocols, leaving their capabilities across construction levels unclear. We propose Frontier3DBench, a unified benchmark of 145 tasks across 9 categories spanning object, scene, and interactive open-world creation, with joint evaluation of appearance, structure, and behavior. Experiments with 11 model-harness configurations reveal strengths that vary by level: GPT-6.1-sol leads the object and scene levels and achieves the highest overall score of 66.02/100, whereas GPT-6-astra leads interactive world construction. However, all configurations score lower on reference reconstruction than on text-driven generation in object and scene tasks. Producing plausible content thus remains easier than reproducing specified geometry, layouts, and visual details. Moreover, generated worlds average 83.08/100 on local mechanisms but only 20.82 on motion clearance and 30.26 on stateful workflows: individual mechanisms often function, whereas complete activities that require coordinated actions and persistent state remain difficult. These results identify reference fidelity and coordinated activity completion as central bottlenecks for coding agents in 3D creation.

items.title: OmniLatent: Unified Latent for 3D Part Modeling
items.summary: 3D part decomposition is a central capability for editable asset creation, yet existing workflows typically segment a completed mesh as a post-processing step, making the…
items.aiSummary: OmniLatent jointly models geometry, deformation, appearance, and part identities in a shared latent space to generate and interactively edit part-aware 3D assets from images or point prompts.
items.abstract: 3D part decomposition is a central capability for editable asset creation, yet existing workflows typically segment a completed mesh as a post-processing step, making the result sensitive to geometric artifacts, texture ambiguity, and limited part-level annotations. We present OmniLatent, a unified latent modeling framework for 3D part decomposition. Instead of predicting part labels in isolation, OmniLatent learns a shared latent space that jointly encodes geometry, deformation, appearance, and binary part IDs, allowing data-rich geometric and visual priors to support data-scarce part learning. Given a single input image, the base model generates geometry, deformation, texture, and surface part IDs in one pass, producing a part-aware 3D asset without a separate segmentation stage. We further tune the pretrained model for two extensions: a point-prompt adapter that maps arbitrary 3D point prompts with binary part IDs into latent tokens for full segmentation, refinement, and part subdivision, and an amodal part completion model that completes partial surface masks into a coherent full-object decomposition through dynamic per-part token allocation, cross-attention to the given geometry latent, and alternating part-local and global attention. Extensive experiments show that OmniLatent produces semantically meaningful part segmentations with precise boundaries, supports interactive part editing, and completes partial part observations while preserving global object consistency.

items.title: Video-Coder: Reinforcing Agentic Coding for Video Generation
items.summary: Recent years have witnessed remarkable progress in video generation in terms of visual quality and temporal consistency. However, generating videos with precise spatial structure, coherent…
items.aiSummary: Video-Coder is a code-driven video generation agent that writes and executes code to build structured 3D draft videos, then uses supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with execution and video rewards to improve controllable video generation.
items.abstract: Recent years have witnessed remarkable progress in video generation in terms of visual quality and temporal consistency. However, generating videos with precise spatial structure, coherent motion dynamics, and controllable scene composition remains challenging. In this paper, we introduce Video-Coder, the first attempt to train a code-driven video generation agent, which autonomously writes and executes code to construct a dynamic 3D scene (Draft Video) that provides structure and motion signals to downstream video generators. To support this paradigm, we design a dedicated data pipeline and curate two high-quality datasets, Video-Coder-SFT-6k and Video-Coder-RL-2k, which contain diverse prompts and ground-truth reference videos. We further develop the Video- Coder Harness, a unified interactive environment integrating code execution, 3D scene rendering, and execution feedback for agent training and inference. We then train Video-Coder with SFT fol- lowed by harness-native agentic reinforcement learning with dual reward feedback, which combines execution-based and video-based rewards. Additionally, we design an annealing training strategy that gradually reduces the execution reward over time, allowing the model to rely more on the video reward in the later training stages. Experiments show that Video-Coder achieves significant gains, improving Minimax-H3 by approximately 7 points on PhyGenBench and 24 points on VBench-2.0. We hope this work can serve as an open foundation for coding agents in video generation, and we fully open-source our data, models, and code

items.title: Exploring Weight-Space Programming: Capabilities, Generalization, and Limitations
items.summary: Weight-Space Programming (WSP) enables reasoning agents to directly inspect and modify neural network parameters, offering an alternative to gradient-based model adaptation. However, its capabilities, cross-task…
items.aiSummary: Weight-Space Programming can produce large localized accuracy gains and uneven cross-task transfer, but reliable editing remains inconsistent.
items.abstract: Weight-Space Programming (WSP) enables reasoning agents to directly inspect and modify neural network parameters, offering an alternative to gradient-based model adaptation. However, its capabilities, cross-task generalization, and practical limitations remain insufficiently understood. We systematically investigate WSP through 16 editing trajectories across seven benchmarks and two model scales (Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-9B). Our findings reveal three key insights. First, WSP can achieve substantial performance gains through highly localized interventions. On full held-out evaluations, accuracy improves by up to 29.45, 4.42, 36.72, and 17.11 percentage points on MATH-500, GPQA Diamond, IFEval, and SciBench, respectively. Notably, modifying only 1,023 parameters yields a 29.45-point improvement. Second, WSP exhibits promising but uneven cross-task generalization. A Math-edited checkpoint improves GPQA Diamond, IFEval, and SciBench by 3.03, 12.18, and 20.10 points, respectively, without further editing, while leaving SciCode performance unchanged. Third, effective editing remains challenging and inconsistent. Outcomes vary substantially across trajectories, and six of the 16 trajectories retain the original weights when candidate improvements cannot be reliably validated. Together, these results highlight WSP's potential for highly localized model adaptation while revealing important challenges in intervention discovery, reliability, and cross-task transfer. Homepage: https://wsp-scope.github.io/ GitHub: https://github.com/WSP-Scope/WSP-Scope-Project

items.title: ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts
items.summary: Reproducing machine learning experiments requires reconstructing procedures from information scattered across papers, released code, and supporting artifacts. For coding agents, reproduction success can therefore depend…
items.abstract: Reproducing machine learning experiments requires reconstructing procedures from information scattered across papers, released code, and supporting artifacts. For coding agents, reproduction success can therefore depend on their ability to fill in missing details, rather than on the released artifacts alone. We ask whether preserving recovered procedures and decisions improves subsequent independent reproduction. We define a standardized artifact design comprising a refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide, and introduce ReproBridge, an agent workflow for constructing these refined reproducible artifacts. ReproBridge-Bench provides 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, anchored by five human-verified reference scores per task. Agents attempt tasks in fresh sessions with raw code or refined artifacts; a separate Auditor checks execution evidence. Across four evaluated models, refined artifacts raise mean reproduction success from 76.4% to 92.6% and reduce downstream API spending by 19.7% on average. The cross-model success-rate spread narrows from 21.6 to 3.9 percentage points, with all four models achieving mean success rates above 90%. Removing any component reduces success in the ablation study, with the largest losses from code and environment removal. These results suggest that preserving execution knowledge helps even models with lower raw-code success reproduce experiments more reliably and at lower API cost.

items.title: AutoCompress: Automated Hardware-Guided Model Compression
items.summary: LLM pruning must preserve quality while meeting hardware- and workload-specific constraints on latency, throughput, and memory. Existing pruning workflows often target parameter counts, requiring practitioners…
items.aiSummary: AutoCompress is a hardware-guided compression framework that uses differentiable architecture search to optimize global and per-layer structures under serving constraints, improving accuracy over Minitron and compressing a large model while retaining most benchmark performance.
items.abstract: LLM pruning must preserve quality while meeting hardware- and workload-specific constraints on latency, throughput, and memory. Existing pruning workflows often target parameter counts, requiring practitioners to manually select model sizes that meet latency, throughput, and GPU memory limits. However, parameter count alone does not predict these metrics, which depend on the model architecture, workload, hardware, and serving engine. We introduce AutoCompress, a hardware-guided compression framework that directly incorporates such constraints into differentiable architecture search. AutoCompress jointly optimizes global and per-layer structure to produce heterogeneous architectures, guided by serving-engine cost models validated against end-to-end latency, throughput, and memory measurements. We evaluate AutoCompress on long-context local coding, batched datacenter serving, and latency-sensitive in-game interaction. Compared to the state-of-the-art Minitron pruning framework, AutoCompress improves average accuracy across eight benchmarks by 6.57, 2.35, and 0.57 percentage points on RTX 5070, RTX 5080, and H100, respectively. AutoCompress also compresses Nemotron 3.5 Super from 120B to 74B parameters for single-B200 BF16 serving at 128K context, retaining 95% of its mean benchmark score.

items.title: SplatAnything: Gaussian Spacing Normalization for Feed-forward 3DGS across Arbitrary Scenes
items.summary: We identify a key limitation of existing feed-forward 3DGS methods: Gaussian attributes are typically predicted in a radial-distance-normalized space that canonicalizes a global radial statistic…
items.aiSummary: SplatAnything applies Gaussian Spacing Normalization to canonicalize scene-level Gaussian spacing, yielding more consistent supervision and improved feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting under varying scene scales and viewpoints.
items.abstract: We identify a key limitation of existing feed-forward 3DGS methods: Gaussian attributes are typically predicted in a radial-distance-normalized space that canonicalizes a global radial statistic of the reconstructed geometry, while the spacing between neighboring Gaussian centers can still vary substantially across scene scales and camera configurations. This mismatch induces systematic shifts in Gaussian-scale targets, leading to ambiguous supervision. To address this, we propose SplatAnything with Gaussian Spacing Normalization (GSNorm), which canonicalizes a robust scene-level statistic of Gaussian spacing to provide a more consistent spatial reference for Gaussian prediction. To rigorously assess our method, we further establish a systematic benchmark spanning diverse datasets, input sparsity levels, and challenging extrapolated viewpoints. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SplatAnything achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly strong gains under substantial variations in scene scale and viewpoint.

items.title: FewStepRL: Fine-tuning Few-step Diffusion Models with Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a standard post-training method for diffusion models, but most RL objectives roll out the current policy at every iteration, and…
items.aiSummary: Reinforcement learning objectives for diffusion models are reformulated for few-step samplers through x-space transformation, gradient decomposition, and anchor adaptation, yielding modular few-step variants of several methods and showing reward-gradient methods excel with differentiable rewards while DiffusionNFT-style methods achieve high rewards in fewer iterations.
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a standard post-training method for diffusion models, but most RL objectives roll out the current policy at every iteration, and with a many-step sampler these rollouts typically dominate the cost of training. Few-step models cut this cost, yet they model an average velocity over an interval, whereas existing RL objectives are built for an instantaneous velocity with a many-step sampler. We adapt RL objectives to few-step models systematically in three phases, namely a transformation, a decomposition and an adaptation. The transformation to x-space expresses each objective we consider through a common policy prediction, at the clean end by default and at an explicitly marked level for transition or flow-map objectives, so that objectives stated over densities, velocities or rewards become comparable. The decomposition writes the gradient of each of these objectives as the sum of a self-regression toward a reference and a reward augmentation, so that a method reduces, at the gradient level, to a choice of anchors and weights. The adaptation computes each anchor from a few-step model at the end of its transport or along its tangent, with the instantaneous velocity recovered from the network itself or from an auxiliary network. This yields few-step versions of FlowGRPO, AWM, DiffusionNFT, DiffusionOPSD and ReFL in one modular codebase. In our experiments, reward-gradient-based methods are the most effective when the reward is differentiable and its gradient is affordable; otherwise DiffusionNFT-style methods generally reach high rewards in relatively few iterations despite a sometimes higher per-iteration cost. Extra inference steps show no systematic aggregate benefit in our experiments, although selected outputs visibly improve with two to four times as many sampling steps as in training.

items.title: Knowing When to Teach: Learning from Teachable Prefixes in Multilingual Reasoning Distillation
items.summary: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) improves reasoning by training a student on its own reasoning, using the same model conditioned on reference solutions as a teacher. Applying…
items.aiSummary: TOPSD improves multilingual reasoning by using likelihood-based drift detection and verification to decide when teacher supervision should be applied during on-policy self-distillation.
items.abstract: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) improves reasoning by training a student on its own reasoning, using the same model conditioned on reference solutions as a teacher. Applying OPSD to multilingual reasoning requires the teacher to provide useful feedback across languages, even when the student makes mistakes in intermediate steps. We observe a phenomenon we call Teacher Drift: as these mistakes accumulate, the teacher may follow the student's incorrect steps instead of correcting them. Our analysis shows that this shift tends to occur earlier in lower-resource languages. To account for these differences across languages, we propose Teachable On-Policy Self-Distillation (TOPSD), which determines where and whether teacher supervision should be applied to each reasoning trajectory. TOPSD uses teacher-student likelihood to estimate where drift begins and select a prefix for supervision. It then verifies whether the teacher can recover the correct answer from that prefix, applying distillation only to prefixes that pass verification. Experiments on multilingual mathematical reasoning across ten languages and three model scales show that TOPSD consistently outperforms conventional OPSD, particularly in low- and medium-resource languages.

items.title: PCBRouteAgent: How Close Are LLM Agents to Becoming PCB Routing Engineers?
items.summary: Automating printed circuit board (PCB) routing requires coordinating board-level connectivity decisions with geometric execution under strict design rules. Although recent agents can interact with native…
items.abstract: Automating printed circuit board (PCB) routing requires coordinating board-level connectivity decisions with geometric execution under strict design rules. Although recent agents can interact with native routing tools, reliable routing on complex boards remains challenging. We present PCBRouteAgent, a multimodal PCB routing agent inspired by how human engineers coordinate global strategy with local execution. A Global Routing Planner combines board images and structured electrical and geometric information to specify connection topology, routing order, corridors, and layer transitions. A Detailed Routing Executor realizes these guides through KiCad's native routing engine and performs bounded local recovery. Unresolved failures are returned as structured feedback, enabling targeted guide revisions while preserving accepted routes. We evaluate PCBRouteAgent on 247 synthetic and real-world boards from four PCBWorld-Bench test splits. It achieves clean-pass rates of 100%, 94.9%, 100%, and 40% on D2, D3-A, D3-B, and D3-C, respectively. On the three real-world subsets, PCBRouteAgent outperforms the best evaluated baseline in clean-pass rate by 13.9, 36, and 10 percentage points, respectively.

items.title: Static Recovery Is Not Dynamic Stability: Dynamics-Aware Benchmarking of Protein Motif Scaffolding
items.summary: Protein motif scaffolding benchmarks assess whether generative models can build scaffolds around functionally important residues. Their conclusions depend on which motifs are tested and which…
items.aiSummary: New benchmarks and molecular dynamics frameworks are presented to rigorously evaluate protein scaffold-generation models by assessing dynamic fidelity and structural stability beyond static success.
items.abstract: Protein motif scaffolding benchmarks assess whether generative models can build scaffolds around functionally important residues. Their conclusions depend on which motifs are tested and which criteria define success. Existing benchmarks typically use small hand-curated motif sets and static refolding criteria, but protein function often depends on conformational ensembles and transitions. Here, we address both benchmark scope and success criteria. We introduce BILBY-PRO, a systematically derived benchmark of structurally conserved functional motifs from PROSITE-linked experimental structures, comprising 220 cases from 174 PROSITE motif-pattern entries. Evaluating six recent scaffold-generation models reveals distinct patterns in target coverage and unique-solution yield: RFDiffusion and Proteina solve more targets, whereas ESM3 produces more unique successful scaffolds on the targets it solves. We further introduce BILBY-MD, a reference-based all-atom molecular dynamics evaluation framework. Applied to statically solved designs from the original MotifBench benchmark, it compares motif drift, scaffold drift, motif-contact preservation, and motif-dihedral free-energy landscapes against reference simulations. Of 55 statically solved model-problem pairs, 31 satisfy our MD-supported criterion and only 8 pass all checks. Compact, self-contained motifs are often MD-supported, whereas interface-like or context-dependent motifs fail more frequently. Static refolding success therefore provides useful evidence of local motif recovery but does not establish dynamical fidelity of the full scaffold. BILBY highlights three complementary axes of motif-scaffolding evaluation: target coverage, unique-solution yield, and MD-supported dynamical fidelity.

IWIBench: Evaluating Gradient-Free Model Driven Intra-weight Injection
items.summary: Intra-weight injection lets one model change another model's behaviour by editing its weights directly, without gradients. Such edits can range from altering lexical associations to…
items.abstract: Intra-weight injection lets one model change another model's behaviour by editing its weights directly, without gradients. Such edits can range from altering lexical associations to enforcing output formats or updating factual knowledge. Despite growing interest in these approaches, there has been no systematic way to evaluate how well models perform them. We introduce IWIBench, which measures a large editor model's ability to modify the weights of a smaller target model (typically Gemma 3 4B IT) to achieve one of ten classical text-editing objectives while preserving its other capabilities. Editors are limited to four tools for reading and writing weights, with bounded tensor access and a fixed budget for generating and inspecting rollouts. A validator applies each proposed patch in a clean environment and compares the edited model against the unmodified target. Evaluating frontier closed- and open-weight models reveals sharply diverging capabilities, both across models and across tasks. A small number of models, most notably Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, perform far ahead of the rest. The recency of this ability (little of it is evident in GPT-5.6 Sol, for instance), together with qualitative analysis, suggests it has been acquired through recent training. Tasks also vary widely: structured response resisted every attempt, and answer-length control yielded only one successful solution, whereas alias acquisition and recoding proved most amenable. Success in one task family correlated poorly with success in others, indicating an early and uneven capability frontier. We discuss strategies that editors repeatedly adopted and conclude with an outlook on intra-weight injection as an emerging but already potent approach to gradient-free behaviour modification.

items.title: The Last Mile to the Real World: Agent-Native Primitives as Reusable Building Blocks for Solving Real-World Tasks
items.summary: How can an agent handle a real-world task end to end? Frontier models with their own harnesses still fall short on real-world benchmarks: on Terminal-Bench…
items.aiSummary: A harness engineering framework composes reusable LLM-equipped primitives into task-specific graphs, verifies and revises them, and improves agent success on real-world tasks while reducing time and cost.
items.abstract: How can an agent handle a real-world task end to end? Frontier models with their own harnesses still fall short on real-world benchmarks: on Terminal-Bench 4.0, GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex resolves 37.3% of the tasks and Claude Opus 5 with Claude Code 51.8%. These tasks fail at the step from reaching a resource to applying it, which we call the last mile to the real world. Existing approaches put the resource within reach but leave the competence to apply it with the caller, so each harness rebuilds that competence. We introduce agent-native primitives, reusable units that equip a resource with a resident LLM that applies it in context and communicates with other primitives, and HEELO (Harness Engineering around Evolving Agent-Native Primitives for the Last Mile to Real-WOrld Tasks), a harness engineering framework that builds each task's harness from a library of such primitives. HEELO composes the primitives a task needs into a task-specific graph, verifies the result against evidence from the environment, revises the primitives a failure implicates, and admits new or improved primitives after validation. We instantiate HEELO with eight primitive families, each built for one kind of task, and evaluate them on more than twenty benchmarks. Dev-Primitives raise Terminal-Bench 4.0 resolution from 37.3% under Codex to 55.5% on the same backbone, Harness Primitives composed per task raise Terminal-Bench 2.0 Pass@1 from 60.0% for the seed harness to 72.2%, Tool Primitives raise ToolBench pass rate from 55.8% to 75.1%, and Navigation Primitives raise GAIA-Text-103 accuracy from 45.6% to 58.3%. On the 46 real-world tasks of our heelo.dev platform, Claude Opus 5.5 with Claude Code and GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex complete 9 each on their own and 39 and 35 when connected to HEELO through our MCP server, with 1.9times and 2.3times less time and 1.55times lower cost per completed task.

items.title: Beneath the Surface: What We Overlook When We Talk About Agent Evolution
items.summary: Agent harness evolution enables recursive self-improvement (RSI) without updating model weights. We examine whether higher benchmark scores yield reliable, efficient, and transferable improvement. We evaluate…
items.aiSummary: Agent harness evolution can improve benchmark performance without weight updates, but gains are unreliable, costly, and transfer inconsistently, motivating preservation-aware evaluation and EvoAudit revisions.
items.abstract: Agent harness evolution enables recursive self-improvement (RSI) without updating model weights. We examine whether higher benchmark scores yield reliable, efficient, and transferable improvement. We evaluate four methods across harnesses, general and coding tasks. Repeated evaluations, controlled agent expansion, component interventions, and admission replays reveal recurring patterns. All sixteen evolved agents gain previously uncovered tasks while losing previously covered ones. In one general-task case, reliability rises by 5.2 points despite losing ten previously covered tasks. Most reliability gains also increase deployment cost. Specific changes usually outperform generic reminders, but their benefits can change when combined. The highest-scoring agent does not yield the largest mean improvement in any of our four pools, and stricter admission can discard useful alternatives. Transfer selectively preserves gains: coverage usually falls on the general-task target across both harness types and paradigms, but rises on the coding target with the outer-layer-only harness. These findings motivate preservation-aware evaluation, tested decision rules, and explicit applicability conditions. As a constructive follow-up, EvoAudit turns these diagnostics into revisions of select, analyze, mutate, and gate, achieving the best performance.

items.title: LowRAM: Low-Rank Keys and Amortised Values for Composable KV Cache Compression at Test-Time
items.summary: Autoregressive decoding relies on the KV cache, whose memory footprint grows linearly with context length and caps batch size and throughput. Existing post-training methods exploit…
items.aiSummary: A method compresses KV caches by predicting values from keys within each attention head and applying cross-layer low-rank key compression, enabling higher decoding throughput and composability with quantization and eviction.
items.abstract: Autoregressive decoding relies on the KV cache, whose memory footprint grows linearly with context length and caps batch size and throughput. Existing post-training methods exploit redundancy across tokens, layers, and feature dimensions, or lower numerical precision. We identify a complementary axis: within each attention head, values are largely predictable from their corresponding keys. We exploit this with value cache amortisation, which fits a lightweight per-head predictor at test time and stores residuals only for the tokens it reconstructs worst, giving 4times near-lossless value compression. The predictor can be initialised by meta-learning for substantially reduced prefill overhead, or fitted from scratch in settings that allow a one-off cost, such as multi-query inference. We pair value amortisation with cross-layer low-rank key compression to produce LowRAM, an asymmetric compression pipeline that stays close to lossless across three model families. By reconstructing only a selected subset of KV pairs at each decoding step, LowRAM can keep decoding overhead minimal and achieve up to 5times higher peak decode throughput at 4times compression. LowRAM further composes with quantisation and eviction, reaching 26.9times compression at 94.5% of baseline performance on long contexts. These results show that treating keys and values as structurally distinct enables efficient, aggressive, and composable KV cache compression.

items.title: LongBanana: An Expert-Verified Benchmark for Long-Context Multi-Reference Image Synthesis
items.summary: We introduce LongBanana, to our knowledge the first expert-designed and expert-verified benchmark for long-context multi-reference image synthesis in the age of agent-driven image generation. The…
items.aiSummary: LongBanana is an expert-verified benchmark and agent-harness framework for evaluating and improving long-context multi-reference image synthesis through graph-grounded checklists and an RPR workflow.
items.abstract: We introduce LongBanana, to our knowledge the first expert-designed and expert-verified benchmark for long-context multi-reference image synthesis in the age of agent-driven image generation. The task requires retrieving dispersed visual evidence, rejecting distractors, binding entities and relations, and composing one coherent final image from multiple references. LongBanana contains 90 carefully designed tasks organized by a 3-by-3 taxonomy; each task includes about 32 reference images, 20 constraints, and 50 evaluation items, yielding 4,670 expert-specified atomic evaluation items in total. Its graph-grounded evaluation design instantiates each task with reference images and an entity-relation graph, then converts node, edge, and whole-graph obligations into checklist items for Content Fidelity, Relational Binding, and Global Constraint Satisfaction. Reviewed expert labels include a 15% double-labeled subset with 89.4% exact agreement and 0.83 quadratic weighted kappa. We further introduce LongBanana-Gen, an agent-harness framework for long-horizon image generation; experiments show that minimal agent harnesses improve over direct generation, while a ReAct-Plan-Exec-Reflect (RPR) workflow yields harness-dependent gains by strengthening evidence grounding and repair. Together, LongBanana provides an auditable testbed for measuring dense visual evidence use and a shared target for developing stronger agent-driven image-generation systems. Code and data are available at the project page: https://long-banana.com/.

EvoWorld: Towards Out-of-Sight World Evolution in Generative Video Models
items.summary: Generative video models are increasingly used as visual world simulators, yet their primary strength lies in rendering plausible pixels rather than reasoning about how a…
items.aiSummary: EvoWorld combines a vision-language model that maintains and reasons over world state with a segment-autoregressive video renderer to improve event-conditioned causal evolution and revisit consistency in generative video world simulators.
items.abstract: Generative video models are increasingly used as visual world simulators, yet their primary strength lies in rendering plausible pixels rather than reasoning about how a world should evolve. Coherent world evolution requires more than visual fidelity: when an event occurs, a model must infer its consequences for the entities in the world and then render the resulting state. For example, after a wild beast appears, the model should not only depict the wild beast, but also infer whether a nearby person should flee, take cover, or fight back based on the realized scene. Existing diffusion-based video models lack an explicit mechanism for maintaining world state and reasoning over such event-conditioned consequences, often producing visually plausible but behaviorally static or causally inconsistent outputs. To make this reasoning gap concrete and measurable, we propose a new problem, Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution, which requires a model to render an event, reason about its consequences for the evolving world state, and reveal a causally plausible outcome as the world continues to evolve, even out of sight. As a baseline reference solution, we introduce EvoWorld, a brain-renderer collaboration framework in which a vision-language model serves as the world brain: it observes generated segments, maintains an evolving account of the world, and reasons about plausible state transitions, while a segment-autoregressive video renderer realizes them visually. We further introduce EvoWorld-Data and EvoWorld-Bench for training and evaluating event realization, causal reactions, and revisit consistency. Experiments show that EvoWorld substantially improves event-conditioned causal evolution over recent models while preserving visual quality and consistency, establishing a reference point for reasoning-guided, autonomous world evolution beyond the current field of view.

items.title: Signed but Steerable: Measuring and Closing the Text-Vector Integrity Gap in Offline Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.summary: Offline retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on edge devices is updated through signed knowledge packs that carry text and precomputed embedding vectors. A signature proves who published…
items.aiSummary: Signed retrieval packs can pass authenticity checks while their embedding vectors are manipulated, so verifiers must validate text-vector consistency and quantisation codes to prevent retrieval hijacking on edge devices.
items.abstract: Offline retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on edge devices is updated through signed knowledge packs that carry text and precomputed embedding vectors. A signature proves who published a pack, not that its vectors encode its text. We study this text-vector integrity gap. A verifier that recomputes vectors and accepts them within a cosine tolerance concedes a predictable share of queries to an attacker who controls the vectors: the hijack rate equals the distribution of angular retrieval margins at the tolerance (the margin law). Margins are small in five corpora and two embedding models, so an idealised tolerance at the level of floating-point noise leaves up to 5.5% of queries exposed (at most 1.2% in any corpus once exact duplicate documents are excluded), and a threshold calibrated from our CPU INT8-FP32 comparison of a small embedding model (at the empirical 0.1% quantile of honest cosines) leaves 98-100% exposed; on a Raspberry Pi 5 running a local language model, such an attack lowers correct answers from 0.75 to 0.39. Integrity audits of compressed vector stores fare no better: on a FAISS product-quantisation index over 57,638 documents, tampered vectors that all pass the audit put the attacker's document first for 25% of targets. Verifying quantisation codes instead, with ambiguity decided by the verifier, a calibrated guard band and canonicalisation, accepted every honest vector in our samples on three platforms and left the publisher no choice. We also show that common floating-point and dynamic-INT8 inference pipelines are not bit-reproducible across batch sizes or architectures, and report pre-registered negative results on abstention, context pruning and semantic screening. We release code and data.

items.title: Confucius4-R2T2: A Stable-Prefix Streaming ASR Model for Real Real-Time Transcription
items.summary: Streaming speech recognition is increasingly consumed by machines, such as translators and voice agents, that act on each token as it appears. A token that…
items.aiSummary: A full-context speech recognizer is adapted to emit immutable streaming transcripts with near full-context accuracy and low latency by learning longest stable prefix labels.
items.abstract: Streaming speech recognition is increasingly consumed by machines, such as translators and voice agents, that act on each token as it appears. A token that is later revised costs wasted work or a wrong action. In this work, we present Confucius4-R2T2 (short for Real Real-Time Transcription), a stable-prefix streaming ASR model that never modifies its earlier output while maintaining high accuracy and low latency. R2T2 is obtained by post-training Qwen3-ASR-1.7B on 1,500 hours of Chinese and English audio while freezing its pre-trained audio encoder and projector. The adaptation is based on the concept of Longest Stable Prefix (LSP), a new notion that we introduce in this work. We prove that LSP is monotone under the prefix order, consistent with the full-audio output, and maximal among labels that equal a whole earlier output. Learning from LSP labels converts a full-context model into a stable-prefix streaming one without any architectural change. Extensive evaluations show that R2T2 brings streaming recognition close to the base model's full-context quality while delivering stable text with low emission lag. Its gains extend beyond the post-training languages, demonstrating a practical path from full-context ASR to stable streaming. We open-source the model weights and code at https://huggingface.co/netease-youdao/Confucius4-R2T2 and https://github.com/netease-youdao/Confucius4-R2T2.

items.title: FlyHash for LLM Agent Memory: An Empirical Validation and a New Application
items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory stores to retain information across conversations, typically via dense vector embeddings searched with approximate nearest-neighbor…
items.aiSummary: FlyHash, a fruit-fly-inspired locality-sensitive hashing method, improves neighbor-structure preservation over SimHash for large language model agent memory retrieval under matched-bit protocols and genuine relevance labels, but it does not provide practical memory or latency advantages over SimHash or HNSW at ordinary scale.
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory stores to retain information across conversations, typically via dense vector embeddings searched with approximate nearest-neighbor methods. The fruit fly's olfactory circuit computes a locality-sensitive hash of sensory input using a strikingly different mechanism - sparse random projection followed by winner-take-all competition - and prior work (Dasgupta et al., 2017) showed this scheme, dubbed FlyHash, preserves neighbor structure better per bit than conventional random-hyperplane hashing (SimHash) on several benchmarks. We apply FlyHash, to our knowledge for the first time, to LLM agent memory retrieval, and ask three questions a practitioner actually needs answered: does the quality advantage hold under a correctly matched-bit protocol (it does, robustly, across 10 seeds and four datasets spanning two modalities, with one specific, previously undocumented comparison pitfall identified and corrected along the way); does that advantage translate into real memory and latency savings, including against the dense-vector indexing (HNSW) practitioners default to today (no: at equal bits FlyHash's codes are larger and slower to compare than SimHash's, and HNSW dominates both hash methods at ordinary scale; a sparse-set comparison we introduce recovers most but not all of a naive latency gap, leaving hashing's practical case narrower and more specific than the quality result alone implies); and does the advantage survive genuine, non-circular agent-memory relevance labels rather than the nearest-neighbor-by-embedding proxy this literature otherwise relies on (it does). We report all three answers precisely, including the two that narrow rather than flatter the headline result, and release our implementation, a working agent-memory demo, and a full account of the methodological pitfalls we found and corrected.

items.title: Where to Connect? Boosting MLLMs via Dynamic Gated Pathways across ALL ViT and LLM Layers
items.summary: A central yet under-explored question in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) is where to connect---how visual information from a hierarchical vision encoder should be wired…
items.aiSummary: Dynamic Gated Pathways enables all-to-all adaptive routing between every vision transformer layer and every large language model layer, allowing each LLM layer to select visual granularities and improving multimodal performance.
items.abstract: A central yet under-explored question in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) is where to connect---how visual information from a hierarchical vision encoder should be wired into the layer-wise semantics of a large language model. Mainstream MLLMs inject a fixed single-layer visual representation into the LLM and treat all LLM layers as a single consumer, ignoring that different layers demand different visual granularities. Recent multi-layer fusion methods either compress hierarchical features on the encoder side or rely on predefined sparse or hierarchical layer-to-layer connections, and therefore stop short of modeling adaptive cross-layer interactions between the ViT and LLM hierarchies. We address this gap with DGP (Dynamic Gated Pathways), a routing mechanism that establishes all-to-all connections between every ViT layer and every LLM layer, with each LLM layer dynamically gating its preference over visual layers conditioned on its own semantic state. Built on top of LLaVA-1.5-7B and 13B, DGP delivers consistent gains over the LLaVA-1.5-7B baseline (e.g., +4.2 on SQA^{I}, +3.3 on MM-Vet, +3.1 on VizWiz and LLaVA^{W}) and surpasses prior multi-layer visual fusion methods on most benchmarks. Layer-wise routing analyses further show that different LLM layers do select different visual granularities on demand, supporting both the effectiveness and interpretability of the proposed dynamic gated pathways. The code is available: https://github.com/YingyingYan1/DGP.

items.title: LLMs Don't Know What They Know: Benchmarking Temporal Self-Knowledge for Financial Backtesting
items.summary: Financial backtests of large language models (LLMs) are meaningful only if the model did not already know the outcomes it is asked to predict. Practitioners…
items.aiSummary: A benchmark of dated U.S. financial facts shows that large language models often understate their knowledge and that common safeguards cannot reliably certify that historical backtests are free of information leakage.
items.abstract: Financial backtests of large language models (LLMs) are meaningful only if the model did not already know the outcomes it is asked to predict. Practitioners guard against this by trusting a vendor's stated knowledge cutoff, by asking the model what it knows, or by instructing it to answer as of a past date. To verify whether any of these safeguards can be trusted, we introduce FinDendro, a benchmark of 2,226 dated U.S. facts from 1999 to 2026, covering monthly macroeconomic series, month-end stock prices and Federal Reserve decisions. Each fact yields four prompts: a value question, Recall and Predict questions that pair each candidate value with a claim of knowing or guessing without a declared date, and a Predict question with a historical declared date. Controls for persistence and dominant outcomes keep chance accuracy near 0.27. Results show that for most frontier models, self-reports understate knowledge. GPT-5 answers 76% of controlled facts correctly but claims to know 38%, and answers 61% of the facts it says it does not know. Knowledge claims can persist beyond the measured knowledge boundary, by up to seven quarters, and a declared date removes most of the claims of prior knowledge while leaving accuracy unchanged. Backtests inside a model's training window therefore cannot be certified leak-free by self-report, instruction or stated cutoff. These findings motivate behavioral measurement of temporal knowledge boundaries, and FinDendro provides a benchmark and procedure for selecting backtest periods based on demonstrated factual knowledge.

items.title: Tools Need Not Speak in Text: Latent Context Compression for Agents
items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents typically append raw tool outputs to their context. Over multi-step interactions, long and noisy observations incur substantial context overhead and…
items.aiSummary: A continuous latent context compression model for LLM agents compresses tool observations into latent tokens and uses action-preserving training to reduce token consumption and runtime while improving task performance.
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents typically append raw tool outputs to their context. Over multi-step interactions, long and noisy observations incur substantial context overhead and dilute the agent's attention to task-relevant information. Existing token pruning and summarization methods remain constrained by discrete text representations, limiting the achievable compression ratios. In this work, we challenge the prevailing assumption that agents must consume tool observations as explicit text tokens. To this end, we propose Coca-Cola, a continuous latent context compression model for LLM agents. Coca-Cola compresses tool observations into latent tokens and embeds them into the input embedding space of the agent. We further introduce Action-Preserving Training, which aligns the agent's next-action distributions under full and compressed observations. This trains the compression model to learn action-sufficient latent tokens that retain decision-critical information. Experiments with web-search agents on four QA benchmarks and two model families show that Coca-Cola reduces the agent's token consumption by 70.01%-89.24% and end-to-end runtime by 24.45%-55.97%, while consistently improving task performance. These results suggest that Coca-Cola offers a promising approach for context compression in agents. Our code is available at https://github.com/THU-Agent/Coca-cola.

items.title: Sketchpad: certified exact arithmetic with a small vision-language model
items.summary: Language models are accurate on most long-arithmetic problems, but their accuracy is estimated on samples and carries no guarantee for an unseen input; tool use…
items.aiSummary: A language model with a low-rank adapter and bounded external memory can be certified exact for arbitrary-length arithmetic by checking finitely many views, and it performs multiple exact arithmetic procedures on a laptop browser.
items.abstract: Language models are accurate on most long-arithmetic problems, but their accuracy is estimated on samples and carries no guarantee for an unseen input; tool use is exact but moves the computation outside the network. We show that exactness at all input lengths becomes a finite, checkable property of a network when each of its steps reads only a bounded view of an external working memory. In Sketchpad, Qwen3.5-0.8B with a low-rank adapter executes arithmetic procedures on a rendered sheet. Each forward pass reads a three-cell view and emits one step: a digit, a carry or borrow, and the next operation. A fixed runtime moves the view and writes no digit of a result. We prove in Lean that the model is then exact on all inputs of any length if and only if it is exact on the finite set of views the runtime presents, that no finite test suffices when steps also read earlier steps, and that the guarantee tolerates bounded numerical perturbation and extends to compositions of procedures. All 2,446 views pass on the deployment device, a laptop GPU running the model in a web browser. The certified model performs signed addition and subtraction, long multiplication and division, square roots and greatest common divisors at arbitrary length. It solved 200 of 200 pre-registered problems in the browser, and 220 of 220 sums of up to 1,000 digits and products of up to 20 digits, of which GPT-6.1 Sol, the strongest of ten other models, solved 217. A symbolic runtime built on these procedures solves, expands and factors polynomials with every number computed by the model, and a multiplicative gate on the adapter recovers the base model exactly when the sheet is not in use.

OneTrans-GSR: A Generative Slate Ranking Paradigm Unifying Reranking and Mix-Ranking with One Autoregressive Transformer
items.summary: Industrial recommender systems allocate substantial computation to pointwise candidate scoring, yet separate reranking and mix-ranking stages still assemble the final exposure slate using hand-crafted rules…
items.aiSummary: A unified decoder-only policy guided by reward-model-based reinforcement learning generates recommendation exposure slates end-to-end, improving business metrics and reducing reranking and mix-ranking latency in a large-scale system.
items.abstract: Industrial recommender systems allocate substantial computation to pointwise candidate scoring, yet separate reranking and mix-ranking stages still assemble the final exposure slate using hand-crafted rules and specialized low-capacity models. Mix-ranking combines product cards, short videos, livestreams, and advertising cards supplied by distinct upstream business channels. Although these rules and models encode valuable domain knowledge, they are inherently limited in leveraging additional data and computation. They constrain the combinatorial space of candidate slates and determine objective trade-offs through manual tuning. To enable scalable and effective slate generation, we reformulate reranking and mix-ranking as a unified learning problem whose performance can improve with computation. Specifically, we instantiate this formulation across the reranking and mix-ranking stages and propose OneTrans-GSR, a single decoder-only policy that extends our deployed OneTrans backbone to generate the exposure slate end-to-end. During training, a reward model evaluates complete slates and guides reinforcement learning toward slate-level and long-term objectives. During decoding, business constraints are explicitly enforced. Offline evaluation shows that slate quality consistently improves as reward-model and policy compute increase. Deployed in a large-scale industrial recommendation system, OneTrans-GSR mixes heterogeneous content types within a unified slate. In online A/B tests, it improves GMV/u by 2.63%, advertiser value by 2.06%, and repurchase rate by 2.03%, while reducing end-to-end latency across the reranking and mix-ranking stages by 13%. These results mark a paradigm shift in slate generation: moving beyond human-engineered heuristics toward a general learned policy creates a scalable path for further algorithmic optimization and compute-driven improvement.

## What's new

* DeepSeek-V4.1 on GB300 gets up to 1.5x more prefill throughput under load and about 28% lower first-token latency on 32K to 64K prompts ([#44403](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/44403), [#45059](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/45059), [#45107](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/45107)).
* SGLang low-latency mode: the opt-in NVIDIA [megakernel](https://github.com/sgl-project/sgl-nvidia-mega) and AMD [monokernel](https://github.com/sgl-project/sgl-amd-mono) plugins run DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash decode as fused persistent kernels, for up to 44% faster single-user decode on GB300 and 75% on MI350X ([#44945](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/44945), [#45450](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/45450), [#44353](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/44353), [#44621](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/44621)).
* MoE models such as DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash and gpt-oss reach the first token 30% to 58% sooner on 8K prompts on H200 ([#43363](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/43363)).
* Paged Experts (opt-in) runs MoE models larger than GPU memory on a single consumer GPU, up to 30x faster than CPU offload ([#42557](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/42557), [#45787](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/45787)).
* SGLang now runs on Google TPU7x through [SGLang-TorchTPU](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-torchtpu), a PyTorch-native plugin for TPU.
* You can now serve LoRA adapters on quantized MoE models (FP8 and NVFP4) with a new opt-in LoRA engine ([#45892](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/45892)).
* DeepSeek-style MLA models running decode context parallelism can now keep their prefix cache in HiCache file-based L3 storage ([#41187](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41187)).

```bash
uv pip install --prerelease=allow sglang==0.5.23
```

| Google TPU7x (TorchTPU) | `docker pull lmsysorg/sglang:v0.1.0-tpu` |

items.aiSummary: P^2-MOPD jointly optimizes mixing coefficients and student weights under an on-policy distillation objective, enabling faster and more balanced recovery than MOPD by treating experts as parameter priors while keeping the student trainable.
items.abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation consolidates expert capabilities by supervising student-generated trajectories, whereas task arithmetic offers a training-free alternative through linear parameter combinations. We view the linear combination of student and expert parameters as a single differentiable model and propose P^2-MOPD, which jointly optimizes the mixing coefficients and the student weights under the same on-policy distillation objective. Unlike task arithmetic, which stays within the span of the frozen student and expert parameters for any choice of merging coefficients, P^2-MOPD keeps the student trainable, so the experts act as parameter priors without confining it to this span. Across four domains at 1.7B and 4B scales, P^2-MOPD achieves faster and more balanced recovery than MOPD from the same initialization, surpassing its final average recovery in half the training steps. At the end of training, our 1.7B model reaches 94.7% average recovery, versus 80.9% for MOPD.

# v0.33.0

## Highlights

This release features 927 commits from 389 contributors (122 new)!

* **New models**: Reflection Beam-1.0 (501B MoE, 23B active) with its DFlash2 drafter (#62074), Yandex AliceAI-Foundation-80B-A3B (#57963), Recursive Flint (40B MoE, 2.5B active) (#62938), Muse Spark Open (#61879), Step-5 Preview (#61727, #63147), NVIDIA Alpamayo 2 Super (#62957), Nemotron-Labs Dory1.0-4B (#60149), Nemotron Parse 3.5 (#61651), MiniCPM-OCR 1.0 (#63095), Domyn Edge (#62544) and the ColUltraVBERT visual document retriever (#62237).
* **PyTorch 2.14**: vLLM is upgraded to PyTorch 2.14.0, with torchvision 0.29.0 and Triton 3.8.0 (#52183).
* **CUDA 12.9 dropped**: release wheels and images are CUDA 13.0 only. The CUDA 12.9 wheels and the `-cu129` / `-cu129-ubuntu2404` images are no longer published (#62575); use the default CUDA 13.0 artifacts instead.
* **libtorch ABI stable CUDA wheel**: the CUDA wheel is now ABI stable with libtorch.
* **AWS EFA image**: a new `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.33.0-efa` image (x86_64 and aarch64) bundles the AWS EFA libraries and the EFA build of the Mooncake transfer engine, for KV transfer and multi-node serving on EFA-enabled EC2 instances (#58768).
* **`vllm/vllm` image alias**: every release image is now also published under the shorter `vllm/vllm` name, e.g. `vllm/vllm:v0.33.0`, `vllm/vllm:v0.33.0-efa` and `vllm/vllm:v0.33.0-rocm`.
* **Speculative decoding**: the new XPress refiner for block-diffusion drafters such as DFlash and DSpark (#54448); FLy, an opt-in lossy verification policy with 1.04-1.31x decode throughput on MI355X and B300 (#53987); DFlash/DSpark no longer reserve draft slots in the token budget, taking DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash + DSpark on GB300 from 1373 to 3390 output tok/s in the PR's benchmark (#59468); quantized draft `lm_head` (`draft_lm_head_quantization`, +18% decode at concurrency 1) (#59973); lookahead block hashes so EAGLE/MTP prefix-cache hits keep their last block, on by default (#61589); and MTP drafts in the Transformers modeling backend (#61270).
* **Faster decode on NVIDIA**: opt-in latency-specialized decode on GB300 for Kimi-K3 (1.5-2x at TP8/TP16, #61867) and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (18.3% faster decode step at batch 1, #61868); DeepSeek-V4/V4.1 MXFP4 experts run as block FP8 through Humming on Hopper (+9-21% decode on 4x H200, #61875); FA4 sparse MLA decode on Blackwell (#55866); FlashInfer DCP prefill on trtllm-gen with 39-48% lower mean TTFT at 100k input on 8xB200 (#62029); and decode-only full CUDA graphs under MRV2 prefill context parallelism (2.6x over eager, #62377).
* **AMD ROCm**: the default ROCm image and wheels move to ROCm 10.0, with ROCm 7.2 still published as `-rocm72` (#58761); MonoKernel decode via `--monokernel` for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on MI300X/MI325X (2.32x P50 interactivity at concurrency 1, #60731) and on every MI355X layer (#61082), and for MiniMax-M3-MXFP4 on MI355X (16.6% lower TPOT, #62712, #62994); the `ROCM_OCTAVE` 3-4 bit KV cache (4.6x the KV tokens of fp16 on RX 7900 XTX, #59774); and gfx1250 enablement for gpt-oss-120b, DeepSeek-R1, DeepSeek-V4-Flash and MiniMax-M3 (#58800).
* **API and serving**: the OpenAI-compatible `/v1/decisions` endpoint, on by default for supported generation models (#60465, #61550); token embeddings with optional late chunking on `/v1/embeddings` (#61772, #63051, #60164); `output_mode="derender"` on `/inference/v1/generate` (#60082); a large Rust frontend parity push, including no more HTTP 500 on long conversations (#62374) and unsupported flags failing at startup (#62431); concurrent worker startup with TP > 1 (#60028); and a watchdog that dumps stack traces from stuck engine and worker processes (#55700).
* **Breaking changes**: Medusa and the MLP speculator removed (#61701); the legacy Ray compiled-graph executor removed (#61712, #62228); `--mamba-cache-mode` deprecated (#60043); requests sent while generation is paused now get HTTP 503 (#51488); the NIXL connector needs NIXL 1.5 or newer (#61032); LM Format Enforcer and `--ir-op-priority` deprecated (#63423, #63371).

## Release Artifacts

<!-- TODO: verify every URL and tag after publishing (wheels.vllm.ai/rocm/0.33.0/, wheels.vllm.ai/0.33.0/xpu, Docker Hub tags, GitHub release assets). -->

### Python Wheels

| Platform | Install |
|---|---|
| PyPI (CUDA 13.0) | `pip install vllm` |
| PyPI (CUDA 13.0, uv) | `uv pip install vllm --torch-backend=auto` |
| ROCm 10.0 | `pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/rocm/0.33.0/rocm100` |
| ROCm 7.2 | `pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/rocm/0.33.0/rocm72` |
| XPU | `uv pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/0.33.0/xpu --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/xpu --index-strategy unsafe-best-match` |

### Docker Images

| Platform | Docker Image |
|---|---|
| CUDA 13.0 (Default) | `docker pull vllm/vllm-openai:v0.33.0` |
| CUDA 13.0 + AWS EFA | `docker pull vllm/vllm-openai:v0.33.0-efa` |
| ROCm 10.0 | `docker pull vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:v0.33.0` |
| ROCm 7.2 | `docker pull vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:v0.33.0-rocm72` |
| CPU | `docker pull vllm/vllm-openai-cpu:v0.33.0` |
| XPU | `docker pull vllm/vllm-openai-xpu:v0.33.0` |

Every image is also available under the shorter `vllm/vllm` name: `vllm/vllm:v0.33.0`, `vllm/vllm:v0.33.0-efa`, `vllm/vllm:v0.33.0-rocm` (`-rocm100`, `-rocm72`), `vllm/vllm:v0.33.0-cpu` and `vllm/vllm:v0.33.0-xpu`. `latest` works the same way, e.g. `vllm/vllm:latest-rocm`.

### Other Artifacts

Pre-built release artifacts are available in the **Assets** section at the bottom of this page, including:
- Source distribution tarball
- CUDA 13.0 Python wheels for x86_64 and arm64
- CPU Python wheels for x86_64, arm64, and macOS
- XPU Python wheel for x86_64

## Model Support
* **New models**: Reflection Beam-1.0 (`BeamForCausalLM`) day-0 support with its DFlash2 drafter and fused Blackwell kernels (#62074, #62042), plus `beam` reasoning and tool parsers (#62052); Yandex AliceAI-Foundation-80B-A3B (Kimi Delta Attention hybrid, 512-expert MoE, 262K context) (#57963); Recursive Flint BF16 and NVFP4 GGUF checkpoints with small-batch Blackwell decode kernels (#62938); Muse Spark Open (#61879) with reasoning and tool parsers (#62207); Step-5 Preview (#61727, #62126, #62132), running on SM100 (#63147) with LoRA (#62498); NVIDIA Alpamayo 2 Super (#62957); Nemotron-Labs Dory1.0-4B (#60149); Nemotron Parse 3.5 with an MTP proposer on MRV2 (#61651); MiniCPM-OCR 1.0 (#63095); Domyn Edge (#62544); ColUltraVBERT (#62237); LFM2.5-Embedding-350M (`Lfm2BidirectionalModel`, #62201); Kolibri 1 through the Transformers backend (#60827); and Decision 3.0 models (#61565, #61778) and Cloudflare Clef-Flash (#61308) on `/v1/systemone`.
* **DeepSeek-V4 and V4.1**: length-aware decode indexer block selection (about 850 us saved per step at 1M context, #61039); MegaMoE experts loaded directly in the DeepGEMM layout so `reload_weights` works (#60096); `fused_wqa_wkv` split by token across TP on SM90 (#58872); MegaAttn `wo_a` writes MXFP8 input for `wo_b` (#60118); native small-head FlashMLA sparse prefill on SM90 (#61615); FlashMLA interleaved KV layout (#61371); redundant EPLB expert slots loaded (#59611); GPU Engram tables read from peer HBM, fixing DEP decode hangs on GB200 (#62091); and fixes for Engram under PP (#62208), Engram all-to-all hangs (#62269), prefill index-workspace NaNs (#60613), C128 compressed-KV writes under PIECEWISE graphs (#59709), routed-expert rows under replay (#61643, #62652) and the updated 1017 reference encoding (#62199, #62200).
* **GLM**: GLM-5.3-Flash defaults to an FP8 KV cache (9.8% higher end-to-end throughput in the PR's benchmark, #61228) and gets mHC TileLang decode kernels on Blackwell (#62745); GLM-5.3 per-token-group quant (2.8% ITL, #60927), in-place draft decode metadata (#61873) and skipped `concat_and_cache_mla` scales (1.2-3.0% TPOT on B300, #62102); FP8 indexer WK pairs kept across `load_weights` calls, fixing thinking loops with runai_streamer (#59223).
* **Kimi-K3**: KDA RecoverSSM CuTe DSL verify/commit kernels on SM10x, with verify records moved out of the KV cache so KV connectors work (#63045); online quantization of NVIDIA projections (#62980).
* **Qwen**: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next FP8 QSA KV cache on Ampere (#60602, #60992), packed NVFP4 PLE embeddings that fit Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 on one DGX Spark (#56273) and PLE short-conv prefill checkpoints (#61601); FlashInfer GDN prefill checkpoints for Qwen3-Next / Qwen3.5 (#60050).
* **Other models**: Cohere2MoE attention/MoE dual stream, single TP all-reduce and fused add + RMSNorm (1.14-1.36x TPOT, on by default, #62101); Beam TP all-reduce fused with norms and MoE finalize (#62366); MiniMax-M3 CUTLASS MSA decode crossover (#55838); Granite MoE as an EAGLE3/DFlash/DSpark target (#61110); NemotronHMTP sharing target embeddings (#62194); LoRA for BERT cross-encoders and token classification (#61279, #61391).
* **Multimodal**: PaddleOCR-VL batched vision encoder (34-85% more throughput, #61458) and `compile_mm_encoder` (#61838); DeepSeek-VL2 ViT full CUDA graphs (#46005); Gemma4Unified batched embedding (#60643); Pixtral real-valued RoPE under compile (#63145); and fixes for EXAONE-4.5 images (broken since v0.29.0, #61104), Gemma 4 encoder graphs (#61365, #60687, #63538), DeepSeek-VL2 encoder cache and PP (#63120, #63192) and Gemma 4 placeholders (#61196).
* **Transformers modeling backend**: MTP speculative drafts (#61270), fused post-top-k MoE routers (#57410), graph caching instead of AOT caching (#58918) and dynamic-RoPE CUDA graphs (#58064).

## Engine Core
* **Speculative decoding**: XPress (#54448), FLy (#53987), no draft-slot budget reservation for DFlash/DSpark (#59468), quantized draft `lm_head` (#59973), lookahead block hashes (#61589), MRV2 skipping drafts no request can use (up to 7.3% prefill throughput with DFlash, #62784), Triton split-K verify (#56148), varlen Mamba2 decode for adaptive verification (#53036), and fixes for stop-trimmed token counts (#58668), block verification randomness (#61161), MTP block tables (#61174), grammar masks (#52477), EAGLE SWA prefix hits (#62206), DFlash/DSpark Mamba checkpoint reuse (#54163) and PP warmup (#62129).
* **Model Runner V2**: batch-sharded sampling for GPT-OSS (#61257) with adaptive verification (#58466), 31-120x faster long-prompt staged writes on GB200 (#62698), encoder towers skipped on later PP stages (0.58-1.27 GiB per stage, #60238), async scheduling kept for ngram (#62521), `input_ids` on later PP stages (#61016), and memory-profiling fixes (#57926, #58243, #61509, #63431).
* **Sampling**: Triton top-k/top-p skips the cutoff search for masked logits (up to about 8x, #61213); small-batch split top-p (1.22-2.70x on B300, #61996); and fixes for huge logits and boundary ties (#58231, #62046).

items.title: Human-Centred, Risk-Constrained Evaluation of Financial Document Recognition: Evidence, Critical Errors, and Selective Automation
items.summary: Financial document recognition is often assessed using character and word error rates, although these metrics do not express whether a system preserves the financial facts…
items.abstract: Financial document recognition is often assessed using character and word error rates, although these metrics do not express whether a system preserves the financial facts on which people and organisations act. This paper develops a human-centred, risk-constrained framework for evaluating financial document recognition as evidence recovery and decision support. It defines typed financial facts linked to visible source regions and separates verbatim transcription, deterministic normalization, and business interpretation. A layered quality model covers text, localization, layout, tables, fields, fact correctness, evidence grounding, uncertainty, robustness, and operational performance. Non-compensatory acceptance gates use one-sided uncertainty bounds for critical-field errors, preventing strong aggregate scores from masking failures in amounts, identifiers, signs, periods, or entity associations. Selective automation is formulated as a constrained routing problem that accounts for residual risk, human-review capacity, and review cost. The framework further specifies annotation and adjudication procedures, leakage-resistant benchmark partitions, statistical estimands, subgroup analyses, and a reproducibility card. Formal results establish the limitations of compensatory scoring, the non-zero upper risk bound after zero observed errors, and a loss sensitive decision rule for routing uncertain cases to human review. The contribution is theoretical and methodological; no new model, dataset, or empirical performance result is claimed.
